turns.doctor_question: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hello, Dr. Smith. It's very nice to meet you too. Thank you for fitting me in. Well, as to what brings me in... it's actually been something of a running joke for a while, but it's starting to really bother me, and honestly, it's getting a bit embarrassing at my age. I'm a secondary school teacher—I've been teaching for over thirty years now, so I'm very used to being on my feet, pacing around the classroom, keeping the teenagers engaged, you know how it is. 

But it's when I'm not teaching that it's the problem. I just... I keep getting up. I cannot seem to stay seated when I'm supposed to. I'll be in a long staff meeting, or even just at a nice sit-down dinner with my husband and our friends, and when everyone else is perfectly content just sitting there, I'll suddenly pop up out of my chair. I'll think to myself, oh, I should go refill my coffee right now, or let me just go check that handout on the back table, or I'll just get up and walk to the back of the room for absolutely no reason. And the thing is, none of it is ever actually urgent! The coffee could completely wait. The handout isn't going anywhere. But I just find myself already standing up and moving, and then I look around and everyone else is just sitting there politely, and I realize I'm the only one wandering around the room again. It just feels like I can't stay anchored to the chair when I'm supposed to.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient explicitly states they cannot stay seated during staff meetings or dinners and frequently get up to wander around when remaining seated is expected.

turns.doctor_question: When you find yourself getting up like that, do you feel an internal sense of restlessness or a physical urge that forces you to move, or is it more that you simply feel bored or distracted and decide to get up?
turns.patient_response:
Well, it's definitely more of an internal restlessness, I think. It's like my body just won't accept being still. You know, it's funny you ask about that, because I've been noticing it so much more lately, especially since the house got so much quieter. My youngest just left for college recently—she's out of state, doing wonderfully, but of course, it completely changes the dynamic at home. You'd think, oh, finally, the empty nest, some peace and quiet, time to just sit and relax, right? 

But for me, I just... I can't seem to stop. I will literally move from one thing to the exact next thing without even a moment's pause. I'll be sitting at the kitchen table doing my lesson planning—which, let me tell you, is a whole production with the new district standards this year—and then before I know it, I'm up throwing a load of laundry in the wash, and then I'm rushing out the door to help out at softball practice, and then I get back and I'm immediately standing at the counter chopping food for this community event we have coming up this weekend. 

It's just this constant, endless stream of activity. And the frustrating part is, I will literally promise myself in the morning, I'll say to my husband, "Tonight is the night I am going to just sit on the sofa, put my feet up, and actually rest." I really mean it when I say it! But when the evening comes, that physical urge you mentioned just kicks in. I feel this... this pressure, this need to be in motion, and I just have to be doing something. So when I pop up out of my chair in a meeting or at dinner, it's not really that I'm just bored and deciding to go look for a distraction, it's more that my body simply refuses to stay paused. It's like I have a motor inside me that just doesn't know how to power down, even when I desperately want it to.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient mentions popping up out of their chair in meetings or at dinner.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient explicitly describes feeling an internal restlessness and a physical urge to be in motion.
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient describes a constant, endless stream of activity and explicitly states it feels like having a motor inside that won't power down.

turns.doctor_question: When you feel that physical urge to move, do you notice any specific, uncomfortable sensations in your legs—like crawling, pulling, or tingling—that are relieved by moving around?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, no, it's really nothing like that at all. I know exactly what you mean—I've had friends describe that sort of creepy-crawly feeling, where they feel like bugs are under their skin or their muscles are twitching when they try to sleep, but I don't get any of that. There's no tingling, no pulling, no uncomfortable physical pain in my legs whatsoever. I'm actually very lucky; at sixty, my joints and my legs are in wonderful shape, probably from all those years pacing the hard linoleum floors at the high school! 

But no, when I get that urge, it isn't localized to my legs, and it isn't a physical discomfort that I'm trying to shake off. It's much more... whole-body, I suppose? It’s just this general, buzzing energy. I'll be sitting on the sofa, like I was saying, trying so hard to just watch a simple half-hour television program with my husband, and my legs feel perfectly fine, but my mind just starts telling me that sitting is the wrong thing to be doing. It's this overwhelming sense that I need to be up and engaged in something, anything at all. I'll stand up just because the act of sitting feels impossible to maintain, not because my legs need to be stretched or relieved of some tingling feeling. It's just... I just have to go. But physically, as far as those specific sensations you mentioned, no, I haven't noticed anything like that.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient describes standing up and leaving her seat on the sofa while trying to watch television because sitting feels impossible to maintain.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient describes an overwhelming, whole-body sense of needing to be up and engaged, making sitting feel impossible.
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient describes having a 'general, buzzing energy' and a feeling that she 'just has to go,' which aligns with acting as if driven by a motor.

turns.doctor_question: Looking back at your childhood or your time in school as a young student, do you remember feeling this same type of internal pressure to be constantly moving or struggling to stay in your seat during class?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, my goodness, yes. Yes, absolutely. It is so funny you ask that because, well, being a teacher myself now, I look back at how I must have been for my own teachers, and I just... I really have to apologize to them in my heart, you know? I actually remember my mother keeping all my old elementary school report cards in this big floral shoebox in our hall closet. And every single year, practically without fail, the comments from the teachers were exactly the same. They always wrote that I was a very bright girl, which was lovely, of course, because I always did well with the actual reading and the math, but then right underneath that, they would write that I simply could not stay in my seat. And that I had a terrible time waiting my turn to speak or do anything, really. I just had to be up and involved right that second. 

I remember feeling like the desk was just a suggestion. Like, why sit when I could stand by the window, or go check on the class pet, or see what my friend two rows over was doing? My mother, bless her, she had a great sense of humor about it most of the time. She used to joke with her friends about it. I can still hear her saying it at our kitchen table, joking that I must have worn a permanent path in the school floorboards between my desk and the pencil sharpener before I was even ten years old! 

Because that was my excuse, you see! I would get up and tell the teacher my pencil was dull and I just had to sharpen it. And then five minutes later I would claim the point broke and I had to go back. I was constantly finding these little loopholes to get out of the chair, just to be in motion. It is exactly like what I do now in staff meetings with the coffee! It is the exact same feeling, just wrapped up in a sixty-year-old woman instead of a third grader. It is really quite something when you think about it, how these things just stay with you for decades. I mean, I can picture that old metal crank pencil sharpener perfectly, the one mounted to the wall right by the chalkboard, and the smell of the cedar shavings... I must have emptied that thing for the teacher a hundred times a year just to have a reason to stand up.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient explicitly states that her teachers noted she 'simply could not stay in my seat' and she constantly found excuses to get out of her chair.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient describes a constant need 'just to be in motion' and confirms feeling an internal pressure to move since childhood.
symptom_reasoning.S017: The patient recalls her teachers writing that she had a 'terrible time waiting my turn to speak or do anything'.
